---
title: "Passing Game Fundamentals: Routes, Timing, and Reads"
subtitle: "The shared language of routes, the quarterback's feet as a clock, and the one defender every pass play is built to put in a bind."
description: "The numbered route tree and the routes that live off it (seam, wheel, whip, option, sluggo); how the quarterback's drop (3/5/7 steps under center, 1/3/5 from the shotgun) is timed to the depth of the routes; timing routes; progression reads versus defender reads, half-field versus full-field; the high-low (vertical) and horizontal stretches of a single conflict defender; and the numbers that measure a throw: air yards, YAC and aDOT."
glossary:
  "Route tree": "A numbered menu of the basic routes a receiver can run, drawn as branches off one straight stem. In a common version, 1 to 9 run from the flat to the go, odd numbers break toward the sideline, even numbers toward the middle, and the numbers roughly grow with depth. Numbering varies by team."
  "Flat route": "A route to the flat, the area near the sideline within a few yards of the line of scrimmage. The shallowest outside route (the 1 in many route trees)."
  Slant: "A route that takes one to three steps upfield, then cuts sharply inside at roughly 45 degrees into the space between defenders a few yards past the line (the 2 in many route trees)."
  Hitch: {def: "A route that pushes upfield, stops, and turns back to face the quarterback. Short versions (5–6 yards) are usually called hitches; deeper ones (10–14 yards), which turn back toward the middle, are curls, the 4 in many route trees.", aliases: ["Curl route"]}
  Out: "A route that runs straight upfield, then breaks flat toward the sideline: a quick out at about 5 yards, a deeper out at 10–14 yards (the 5 in many route trees)."
  Dig: {def: "A route that runs upfield and then breaks flat across toward the middle of the field, usually 10–15 yards deep (the 6 in many route trees). Shallower versions are often just called in routes.", aliases: ["In route"]}
  "Corner route": "A route that pushes upfield 10–12 yards, then angles toward the sideline and the far corner of the field or end zone (the 7 in many route trees). Also called a flag route."
  Post: "A route that pushes upfield, then angles deep toward the middle of the field, where the goalposts are (the 8 in many route trees)."
  "Go route": {def: "A straight sprint upfield to run past the defender (the 9 in many route trees).", aliases: ["Fly route", "9 route"]}
  Comeback: "A route that sells a deep route for about 15 yards, then stops and comes back toward the sideline and the quarterback (the 3 in many route trees)."
  Wheel: "A route that starts out toward the flat and then turns up the sideline, usually run by a running back or a slot receiver."
  Seam: "A vertical route up the seam, the strip of field between the hash marks and the painted numbers, usually by a slot receiver or tight end, aimed at the gaps between deep defenders."
  Whip: "A short route in which a slot receiver runs at the middle as if on an in-cut, plants, and snaps back toward the sideline. Built to beat a defender who jumps the first move."
  Sluggo: "A double move: a slant fake ('slant and go'), then straight up the field past the defender who bit on the slant."
  "Option route": {def: "A route on which the receiver picks the finish after the snap from what the coverage does: against man he breaks away from the defender's leverage; against zone he settles in the hole between defenders. The quarterback has to see the same thing.", aliases: ["Choice route"]}
  "Drop (3/5/7-step)": "The quarterback's steps backward from the snap to his throwing spot. From under center, 3-, 5- and 7-step drops end roughly 5, 7 and 9 yards deep; from the shotgun, which starts 5 yards back, the same depths take 1, 3 and 5 steps. Each drop is timed to a depth of route."
  "Timing route": "A route the quarterback throws to a spot at a set moment, as his drop ends and often before the receiver has made his break, so the ball and the receiver arrive together."
  Progression: "The order in which the quarterback looks at his receivers on a pass play, usually tied to the steps of his drop: if the first is covered he moves to the second, and so on down to the checkdown."
  "High-low read": {def: "Putting two receivers in one defender's area at two depths, one above him and one below, and throwing to whichever one he leaves.", aliases: ["Vertical stretch"]}
  "Horizontal stretch": "Putting receivers on both sides of an underneath defender (or spread across the field) at about the same depth, so a zone defender can't cover both and the quarterback throws to the one he leaves."
  "Conflict defender": "A defender who is responsible for two things at once (two receivers in his area, or a run gap and a pass zone), so that whatever he does leaves one of them open. Pass plays and RPOs are built around him."
  "Air yards": "How far past the line of scrimmage a pass travels in the air, to the spot where it is caught (or where the target was when it fell incomplete). Throws behind the line have negative air yards."
  YAC: {def: "Yards after catch: the yards a receiver gains after he catches the ball, from the spot of the catch to the end of the play.", aliases: ["Yards after catch"]}
  aDOT: {def: "Average depth of target: the average air yards per pass thrown by a quarterback, or per target for a receiver. How far downfield, on average, the ball is aimed.", aliases: ["Average depth of target"]}
---

#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
import os
import logging

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch, Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from IPython.display import Markdown

import gridiron.play as gplay
from gridiron import Play, Player, offense, defense, routes as r, show_animation, style, draw_marker

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
FIELD_W = 160 / 3
ODD, EVEN = style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.THIRD      # outside-breaking vs inside-breaking routes


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Remove the painted yard-line numbers (they sit where receivers stand and crowd the labels)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


def ruler(fld, play, top=40, fs=6.5):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) down the left edge of the window, so the
    faint 5-yard lines read as a scale. gridiron has no ruler, so it is drawn here."""
    x_left = FIELD_W - fld.y1 + 0.4
    for d in range(5, top + 1, 5):
        y = play.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 0.8 <= y <= fld.x1 - 0.8:
            fld.ax.text(x_left, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == 5 else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                        ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def tag(fld, play, text, at, ha="center", fs=7.0, ec=style.BASELINE, color=style.INK, bold=False):
    """A boxed label at (d, w) yards; `ec` colours the box edge (used to key route families)."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*at))
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color, zorder=12,
                fontweight="bold" if bold else "normal",
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.22", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ec, lw=0.9))


def dotted(fld, play, pts, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.4, arrow=True):
    """A dotted optional branch through (d, w) points, with an arrowhead."""
    xy = [tuple(float(v) for v in fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*q))) for q in pts]
    xs, ys = zip(*xy)
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=(0, (1, 1.5)), zorder=4)
    if arrow:
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy[-2], xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9, color=color,
                                         lw=0, zorder=4, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))


def protect(p, rushers=("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE")):
    """Five linemen set and four rushers engage them: enough to say 'pass', no more."""
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        if k in p.players:
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    for k in rushers:
        if k in p.players:
            p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)


class ball_speed:
    """Temporarily set gridiron's ball speed (yd/s). Its default, 18, is an average over a whole
    flight; a firm 20-30 yard line drive to the sideline travels faster, so the timing figures use
    20-22. Used as `with ball_speed(22): ...` so other figures keep the default."""
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v

    def __enter__(self):
        self.old = gplay.BALL_SPEED
        gplay.BALL_SPEED = self.v

    def __exit__(self, *a):
        gplay.BALL_SPEED = self.old


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- snapshots (print stand-in for video)
def snapshot(play, t, ax=None, lateral=(-6, 26.6), window=(-9, 20), width_in=6.5, notes=(), rings=(),
             show_ruler=False, numbers_off=True):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, faint trails of where they came from, and the ball in flight."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    lo, hi = sorted(lateral)
    moved = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()
             if lo + 0.8 <= float(pos[k][1]) <= hi - 0.8]          # drop anyone outside the window
    q = Play([m for m in moved if m.side == "off"], [m for m in moved if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    for k in rings:
        q.highlight(k)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, width_in=width_in, title=False)
    ax, ppy = fld.ax, fld.pts_per_yard()
    if numbers_off:
        no_numbers(ax)
    if show_ruler:
        ruler(fld, play, fs=5.5)
    P = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
    t0 = play._compile()[1]
    for k, pl in play.players.items():
        if pl.pos in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT", "DE", "DT", "NT"):
            continue
        pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(t0, t, 40)])
        if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.3:
            continue
        xs, ys = P(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
        if pl.side == "off":
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, alpha=0.5, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
    bx, by = P(*play.ball_position(t))
    for kind, _, t_rel in play.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass" and t > t_rel:
            sx, sy = P(*play.ball_position(t_rel))
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(sx), float(sy)), (float(bx), float(by)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=8, color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9))
    draw_marker(ax, float(bx), float(by), "ball", "", ppy)
    for text, at in notes:
        tag(fld, play, text, at, fs=6.3)
    return fld


def strip(plays, times, labels, lateral=(-6, 26.6), window=(-9, 20), notes=None, rings=(), width_in=6.5,
          ncols=3, legend=True, rulers=True):
    """Panels at chosen moments. `plays` is one Play (used for every panel) or one per row."""
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    if isinstance(plays, Play):
        plays = [plays] * nrows
    pw = width_in / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.34)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times, labels)):
        snapshot(plays[i // ncols], t, ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window,
                 notes=(notes or {}).get(i, ()), rings=rings, show_ruler=rulers and (i % ncols == 0))
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=7.8, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.5, w_pad=0.3)
    if legend:
        h_ = [Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, alpha=0.6, label="Receiver's path so far"),
              Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="Defender's path so far"),
              Line2D([], [], color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), label="Ball in flight")]
        fig.legend(handles=h_, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=3, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
    return fig


def show_videos(plays, titles):
    """Web build: several animations side by side in ONE output, so Quarto keeps a single figure
    (two separate show_animation calls would be split into sub-figures)."""
    import shutil
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    from gridiron.animate import animate
    parts = []
    for pl, ttl in zip(plays, titles):
        anim = animate(pl, title=ttl, to_go=pl.to_go)
        if shutil.which("ffmpeg"):
            html = anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
        else:
            html = anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once")
        plt.close(anim._fig)
        parts.append(f'<div style="flex:1 1 300px;min-width:0">{html}</div>')
    display(HTML('<div style="display:flex;gap:8px;flex-wrap:wrap">' + "".join(parts) + "</div>"))
```

#| label: data-setup
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (load the passing data used in this chapter)"

from gridiron.data import pbp, nfl

SEASONS = range(2021, 2026)          # five completed seasons, 2021-2025
PCOLS = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "play_type", "pass_attempt", "sack", "air_yards",
         "yards_after_catch", "receiving_yards", "complete_pass", "interception", "epa", "success",
         "passer_player_name", "receiver_player_name", "receiver_player_id", "posteam"]
_raw = pbp(SEASONS, columns=PCOLS)
# Pass attempts that were actually thrown at someone: regular season, sacks out, and only rows
# with a charted air-yards value (spikes and most throwaways have none).
passes = _raw[(_raw.season_type == "REG") & (_raw.play_type == "pass") & (_raw.pass_attempt == 1)
              & (_raw.sack == 0) & _raw.air_yards.notna()].copy()
DEPTH_BINS = [-100, -0.5, 4.5, 9.5, 14.5, 19.5, 29.5, 100]
DEPTH_LABS = ["Behind\nLOS", "0-4", "5-9", "10-14", "15-19", "20-29", "30+"]
passes["depth"] = pd.cut(passes.air_yards, DEPTH_BINS, labels=DEPTH_LABS)

# FTN charting (2022+) says which read each pass went to; participation gives time to throw.
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()
ftn["read_thrown"] = ftn.read_thrown.astype(str).str.strip()
part = nfl().load_participation([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]).to_pandas()[["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "time_to_throw"]]
p22 = pbp([2022, 2023, 2024, 2025], columns=PCOLS)
p22 = p22[(p22.season_type == "REG") & (p22.play_type == "pass") & (p22.pass_attempt == 1) & (p22.sack == 0)]
reads = (p22.merge(ftn[["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id", "read_thrown", "is_throw_away", "is_screen_pass",
                        "is_qb_out_of_pocket"]],
                   left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "nflverse_play_id"], how="inner")
         .merge(part, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"], how="left",
                suffixes=("", "_p")))

# Numbers quoted in the text
_r25 = reads[reads.season == 2025]
TTT25 = _r25.time_to_throw.median()                                    # median snap-to-throw, 2025
_p25 = passes[passes.season == 2025]
LG_ADOT_25 = _p25.air_yards.mean()
_c25 = _p25[_p25.complete_pass == 1]
YAC_SHARE = _c25.yards_after_catch.sum() / _c25.receiving_yards.sum()
_db = pbp([2025], columns=["season_type", "qb_dropback", "shotgun", "play_type"])
_db = _db[(_db.season_type == "REG") & (_db.qb_dropback == 1) & _db.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])]
GUN_DB_25 = _db.shotgun.mean()                                         # dropbacks from shotgun/pistol
```

Second-and-8 near midfield. The quarterback takes the snap under center, takes five quick steps
backward, plants, hops forward once, and throws toward the sideline, to a patch of grass where
nobody is standing. The receiver he is throwing to is still sprinting straight up the field, with the
cornerback backpedalling in front of him. A beat later the receiver snaps his head around, cuts hard
toward the sideline, and the ball arrives at that patch of grass at the same moment he does, a step
ahead of the cornerback. The analyst says "that's timing." What does that mean? How did the
quarterback know where to throw before the receiver got there? Why five steps and not three or
seven? And when the cornerback *does* get there first, how does the quarterback decide to throw
somewhere else instead? This chapter is about the three things that make every pass play work: the
**routes** (where the receivers go), the **drop** (when the ball comes out), and the **read** (who
gets it).

**You'll be able to…**

- Name every route on a replay, by its common name and its number in the route tree, including the
  routes that live off the tree: seam, wheel, whip, option and sluggo.
- Count a quarterback's drop, from under center or from the shotgun, and say roughly how deep the
  throw is meant to be and when it should come out.
- Tell a progression read from a defender read, and a half-field read from a full-field read.
- Find the conflict defender in a high-low (vertical) stretch or a horizontal stretch, and say which
  receiver he left open.
- Read air yards, YAC and aDOT in a box score or a chart, and say what each one tells you about an
  offense.

*Reading the diagrams:* offense is blue circles (Q quarterback, R running back, C center; X, Y, Z
and H are receivers: X the wide receiver on the line, Z the wide receiver off it, Y usually the tight
end, H the third wide receiver). Defense is orange outlined squares: E and T defensive ends and
tackles, M and W the Mike and Will linebackers, S the Sam linebacker, \$ the nickel back (the slot
cornerback), CB a cornerback, FS and SS the free and strong safety. Solid arrows are routes, dashed
orange arrows are defenders' drops into zones, a dotted line is an optional path, and a T-shaped end
is a block. The dark blue line across the field is the line of scrimmage, the orange-yellow line is
the line to gain, the faint lines are 5 yards apart, and the small numbers on the left edge give the
depth past the line. A green ring marks the player to watch. These conventions are the ones
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd) introduced.

## The passing problem: a race against the rush

A pass play has a clock on it, and the defense controls it. Four or more pass rushers start
running at the quarterback at the snap. His linemen can hold them off for a while, but not forever.
In the 2025 regular season the median pass left the quarterback's hand
`{python} f"{TTT25:.1f}"` seconds after the snap (by the data providers' clock; see the note
with the timing chart).[^ttt] That is the whole budget: roughly two and a half seconds for
receivers to get somewhere useful, for the quarterback to decide, and for the ball to leave.

Inside that budget the offense has to solve three problems at once.

1. **Where.** Each receiver needs a path that takes him to open grass, or to a place where the
   defender guarding him is at a disadvantage. That is his **route**.
2. **When.** The quarterback needs to be ready to throw at the moment the receiver gets there, not a
   second before (the defender is still close) and not a second after (the defender has recovered,
   or the rush has arrived). His footwork, the **drop**, is how the two are synchronised.
3. **Who.** Five players can go out for a pass, and the defense will cover some of them better than
   others. The quarterback needs a plan for deciding, in a second or two, which one gets the ball.
   That plan is the **read**.

Every pass concept in the next seven chapters is a particular answer to those three questions. This
chapter builds the vocabulary: the routes, the clock, and the two basic ways to put a defender in a
bind.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In the video game a pass play is five fixed lines, and you choose a receiver by pressing his button
whenever you like. In a real offense a route is a set of instructions that can change with the
coverage, the depth of a route moves with the down and distance (a receiver on third-and-7 runs his
route past the line to gain, not a yard short of it), and the quarterback can't wait until a receiver
looks open. By the time a receiver *looks* open on a television screen, it is usually too late to
throw it to him. Real quarterbacks throw to where a receiver is about to be open, on a count their
feet keep.
:::

## Anatomy of a route

Watch one receiver on one play and you can see four parts to his route.

- **The release.** His first steps off the line, getting past the man in front of him. Against a
  [press](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-press) cornerback standing nose to nose with him, the
  release is a fight of its own; [The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd) covers the
  [release](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-release-vs-press) techniques.
- **The stem.** The run upfield before the cut. A good
  [stem](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stem) looks the same for every route, so the defender
  can't tell from it which way the receiver will break. Receivers also use the stem to push the
  defender back, or to steer toward one shoulder of him.
- **The break.** The cut. Its depth is usually set by rule ("break at 12 yards"), and its direction is
  what names the route.
- **The finish.** What happens after the cut: keep running away from the defender, stop and face the
  quarterback, or settle in a gap between defenders.

The break is the moment that matters. A receiver can't outrun a defender who is backpedalling in
front of him and watching him, but he can make that defender guess. At the break the receiver knows
where he is going and the defender doesn't, so for a fraction of a second the receiver is ahead.
That gap, a yard or two of [separation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-separation) between receiver and defender, closes fast. Everything about timing is about getting the
ball there before it does.

## The route tree: a shared language

Receivers and quarterbacks need to talk about routes quickly, in a huddle or with a hand signal at
the line. Most offenses therefore teach a **[route tree](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-route-tree)**:
a numbered menu of the basic routes, drawn as branches off one straight stem. Here is one common
version, for a receiver on the right side of the formation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-route-tree
#| fig-cap: "One common numbered route tree, drawn for a wide receiver on the right of the formation (the ball is at the bottom left, the right sideline at the right edge). Every route starts with the same push straight up the field and splits at a break point. Odd numbers (dark blue tags) break toward the sideline, even numbers (green tags) toward the middle, and the numbers roughly grow with depth. The 0, the hitch, is an addition some systems make. The table beside the tree lists each route's typical break depth and direction (an arrow means the route keeps climbing after the break)."
W0 = 13.0                                    # the receiver: on the line, just inside the numbers
TREE = [  # number, name, absolute (d, w) waypoints after the start, label spot, label alignment
    (0, "hitch", [(6.0, W0), (5.2, W0 - 0.5)], (5.6, 15.6), "left"),
    (1, "flat", [(1.4, W0 + 1.5), (2.4, W0 + 6.5)], (2.4, 20.4), "left"),
    (2, "slant", [(1.8, W0), (6.6, W0 - 6.2)], (6.6, 6.1), "right"),
    (3, "comeback", [(16.0, W0), (13.6, W0 + 3.0)], (13.6, 16.8), "left"),
    (4, "curl", [(12.0, W0), (10.6, W0 - 1.5)], (9.9, 10.6), "right"),
    (5, "out", [(10.0, W0), (10.0, W0 + 6.5)], (10.0, 20.4), "left"),
    (6, "dig (in)", [(14.0, W0), (14.0, 2.5)], (15.6, 2.4), "left"),
    (7, "corner", [(12.0, W0), (22.0, W0 + 7.0)], (23.8, 19.8), "center"),
    (8, "post", [(12.0, W0), (25.5, W0 - 7.5)], (27.0, 5.5), "center"),
    (9, "go", [(29.5, W0)], (31.0, W0), "center"),
]
off = [Player("C", "C", "off", -0.7, 0.0, label="C"), Player("QB", "QB", "off", -5.0, 0.0, label="Q")]
off += [Player(f"R{n}", "WR", "off", -0.7, W0, label="") for n, *_ in TREE]
off[-1] = off[-1].moved(label="Z")          # draw one labelled marker on top of the stack
tree = Play(off, [], los=35, to_go=None)
for n, name, pts, *_ in TREE:
    tree.route(f"R{n}", pts, absolute=True)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4.35))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, width_ratios=[1.45, 1.0], wspace=0.04)
ax, axl = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
fld = tree.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-6, 26.6), window=(-6.5, 32.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, tree, top=30)
for n, name, pts, at, ha in TREE:
    tag(fld, tree, f"{n}  {name}", at, ha=ha, ec=ODD if n % 2 else EVEN, bold=True, fs=7.2)
tag(fld, tree, "toward the middle", (-4.6, 7.0), fs=6.6)
tag(fld, tree, "toward the sideline", (-4.6, 19.0), fs=6.6)
# the cheat sheet beside the tree
CHEAT = [(0, "hitch", "5-6", "stop, face QB"), (1, "flat", "0-3", "out"), (2, "slant", "3-6", "in, 45°"),
         (3, "comeback", "15 → 12", "back, out"), (4, "curl", "10-14", "stop, face QB"), (5, "out", "10-14", "out, square"),
         (6, "dig", "10-15", "in, square"), (7, "corner", "10-12 →", "out, deep"), (8, "post", "10-14 →", "in, deep"),
         (9, "go", "—", "straight")]
axl.axis("off")
axl.set_xlim(0, 1)
axl.set_ylim(0, 1)
axl.text(0.025, 0.96, "#", fontsize=7.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center", family="DejaVu Sans Mono")
axl.text(0.11, 0.96, f"{'Route':<12} {'Break (yd)':<13} Direction", fontsize=7.2, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
         va="center", family="DejaVu Sans Mono")
for i, (n, name, dep, dirn) in enumerate(CHEAT):
    y = 0.885 - i * 0.07
    axl.text(0.02, y, f"{n}", fontsize=7.6, fontweight="bold", va="center", color=style.INK,
             bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=ODD if n % 2 else EVEN, lw=1.1))
    axl.text(0.11, y, f"{name:<12} {dep:<13} {dirn}", fontsize=7.2, va="center", color=style.INK,
             family="DejaVu Sans Mono")
axl.text(0.02, 0.0, "Box colour: dark blue = odd, breaks toward the\nsideline; green = even, breaks toward the middle.\nDepths in yards past the line; typical, not laws.",
         fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom")
plt.show()
```

Two patterns make the tree easy to remember. **Odd numbers break toward the sideline and even numbers
break toward the middle**, and **the numbers roughly grow with depth**: low numbers are short
routes, high numbers deep ones. The tree is the same on both sides of the field; a receiver on the
left simply mirrors it, so "breaks outside" always means "toward his own sideline." Here are the
branches, each with the reason it exists.

- **1, the [flat route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flat-route).** A quick release to the
  *flat*, the strip of field near the sideline within a few yards of the line. It is the
  shallowest route there is, and its job is often to pull a defender down and out with it, opening
  the space above him. From an outside receiver it looks like a very shallow quick out.
- **2, the [slant](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slant).** One to three steps upfield, then a sharp
  cut inside at about 45 degrees. It attacks the space between the defenders near the line and the
  ones behind them, and it gets the receiver's body between the ball and a defender lined up
  outside him. It is the quickest-developing route in football and a staple when the defense brings
  extra rushers.
- **3, the [comeback](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-comeback).** A hard run upfield for about 15
  yards to sell a deep route, then a stop and a turn back toward the sideline. It exists because
  cornerbacks fear being beaten deep: the more convincing the vertical push, the further the
  cornerback retreats, and the more room the receiver has when he comes back. The throw is long, from
  the middle of the field to the sideline, so it asks a lot of the quarterback's arm.
- **0 and 4, the [hitch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hitch).** Push upfield, stop, and turn
  back to face the quarterback. At 5–6 yards it is usually called a hitch (some trees number it 0, and
  many have no number for it at all); at 10–14 yards, turning back slightly toward the middle, it is a
  **[curl](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-route)**, the 4. Both attack a defender who is
  backing up: when a cornerback lines up 7 or 8 yards off a receiver to protect against the deep
  ball, a 5-yard hitch is open almost by definition.
- **5, the [out](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-out).** Straight up the field, then a square cut
  toward the sideline. A *quick out* breaks at about 5 yards; the deeper out breaks at 10–14. It
  attacks the area outside the defenders who are responsible for the middle, and the sideline stops
  the clock if he steps out. The deep out is the hardest throw in the tree, because the ball has to
  travel the full width from the quarterback to the sideline before the cornerback can come down on
  it.
- **6, the [dig](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dig).** Up the field 10–15 yards, then a flat cut
  across toward the middle. Shallower versions are often called an
  **[in route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-in-route)**. The dig attacks the middle of the
  field behind the linebackers, the area they vacate when they drop or blitz.
- **7, the [corner route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-corner-route).** Up the field 10–12 yards,
  then an angle toward the sideline and the far corner of the field (the pylon at the corner of the
  end zone, which is why some playbooks call it the *flag*). It attacks the deep area outside, above
  a cornerback who stays low and inside a safety who stays in the middle.
- **8, the [post](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post).** Up the field, then an angle deep toward
  the middle, where the goalposts stand. It attacks the deep middle, between deep defenders or behind
  a safety who has come forward. A version that stays more vertical, angling only slightly inside, is the *skinny post*.
- **9, the [go route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-go-route).** A straight sprint up the field,
  also called a **[fly](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fly-route)** or a
  **[9 route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-9-route)**. Its purpose is to outrun the man covering
  him. Even when it isn't thrown, it does a job: a cornerback who has to run with it is no longer
  near the short routes underneath. A go route that drifts toward the sideline to make room for the
  throw is a [fade](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fade), a red-zone favourite ([Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)).

Read the tree in pairs and you can see that each route is the answer to a defender's choice.
The comeback and the go both start the same way: if the cornerback stays deep, the comeback is open;
if he jumps the comeback, the go is. The curl and the corner make the same pair inside a single
stem. That is the whole idea of route design in miniature: make a defender choose, then throw where
he didn't go.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
The tree exists to make calls short and practice efficient. If every route has a number and a fixed
depth, one word or one digit tells a receiver exactly where to go, and a quarterback and receiver
who have run the 5 a thousand times in practice know, without talking, where the ball will be and
when. The cost is rigidity. A number says nothing about how two routes work together, and a fixed
depth is easy for a defense to study. That is why modern playbooks name *combinations* of routes
(concepts) rather than single routes, and why many routes are taught with rules that change their
depth or their break against different coverages
([Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd) compares
the approaches).
:::

### Who numbered the routes

The idea that every route should have a number is usually traced to Don Coryell, who coached San
Diego State from 1961 to 1972 and the San Diego Chargers from 1978 to 1986. Coryell built on Sid
Gillman's passing ideas (Gillman coached the Chargers in the 1960s), whose central principle was to
make a defense cover the whole field, every yard of its width and depth. Coryell's numbering let a
play-caller describe three receivers' routes in a single three-digit call. His Chargers, the "Air
Coryell" teams with Dan Fouts at quarterback, led the NFL in passing yards in six straight seasons
from 1978 to 1983 and again in 1985, and the numbering spread with his assistants and their
assistants through the league.[^coryell] It never became a standard, though. Trees differ from
team to team: some reverse the odd-even rule, some number inside receivers' routes separately, some
call the 3 an out and the 5 a comeback. When you hear "a 9 route," you can be fairly sure it means a
go; most other numbers depend on who is talking.
[Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd) shows how
Coryell's **[digit system](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-digit-system-route-numbering)**
turns the tree into a play call. The route names, on the other hand, are close to universal.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The receiver runs the route as drawn." Routes are drawn as lines, but they are taught as rules,
and the depths in the tree are targets, not laws. A 12-yard out on third-and-14 is run at 14 yards,
past the line to gain. A receiver who sees the defender sitting on the spot where his route ends
may be taught to adjust it, and on some routes the adjustment is the whole point (the option
routes below). The quarterback has to know the rule as well as the receiver does, which is why the
two spend so much practice time together.
:::

## Off the tree: seam, wheel, whip and sluggo

The tree describes what one wide receiver can do from the outside. Receivers who line up inside, in
the [slot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slot) or at tight end, and running backs who start in
the backfield have routes of their own, and so do receivers trying to fool a defender rather than
simply get past him. Four come up constantly.

```{python}
#| label: fig-off-tree
#| fig-cap: "Four routes that live off the tree, from a 2x2 formation (the other routes are left off). Left: the sluggo (X fakes a slant for two steps, then runs straight up the field) and the whip (H runs at the middle as if on a short in-cut, plants, and snaps back out). Right: the seam (Y runs straight up between the hash and the numbers) and the wheel (the back runs to the flat, then turns up the sideline)."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [p.moved(w=-17.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-8.0) if p.key == "H"
       else p.moved(w=8.0, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=17.0) if p.key == "Z"
       else p.moved(w=2.2) if p.key == "RB" else p for p in off]
ot = Play(off, [], los=35, to_go=None)
ot.route("X", r.path((2.0, 0.0), (4.3, -2.2), (25.0, -2.0)))                 # sluggo: slant fake, then go
ot.route("H", r.path((3.0, -0.6), (4.6, -3.0), (4.2, 3.4)))                  # whip: in, plant, back out
ot.route("Y", r.seam(24))                                                      # seam
ot.route("RB", r.path((0.6, 4.5), (2.2, 8.5), (4.6, 10.6), (7.5, 11.2), (24.0, 11.6)), side=+1)  # wheel
ot.dropback(2.0)
fld = ot.draw(lateral=(-22, 20), window=(-7.5, 28.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, ot, top=25)
tag(fld, ot, "sluggo (slant-and-go)", (26.8, -15.0), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "whip", (1.6, -12.6), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "seam", (24.4, 7.6), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "wheel", (21.0, 13.6), bold=True)
tag(fld, ot, "hash", (-6.4, -3.1), fs=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
tag(fld, ot, "hash", (-6.4, 3.1), fs=6.0, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

- **The [seam](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-seam).** A go route from the inside, straight up
  the strip of field between the hash marks and the painted numbers. That strip is the seam between
  defenders' areas: in most deep coverages it sits between the safety in the middle and the deep
  defender outside, so a seam route forces the defense to decide who takes it. It is the slot
  receiver's and tight end's best way to threaten the deep middle.
- **The [wheel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wheel).** A route that starts out toward the flat
  and then turns up the sideline. It is usually run by a running back or a slot receiver, and its
  trick is the change of direction: a defender who sees a back heading for the flat comes forward to
  cover a short route, and the back turns up the field past him. It is especially dangerous when a
  linebacker is covering the back man-to-man, because few linebackers can run with a back up the
  sideline.
- **The [whip](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-whip).** A slot receiver runs at the middle as if on
  a shallow in-cut, plants his inside foot, and snaps back toward the sideline. It is built for a
  defender playing man-to-man who jumps the first move: the harder the defender drives on the in-cut,
  the more open the receiver is when he reverses.
- **The [sluggo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sluggo).** "Slant and go": a two-step slant fake,
  then straight up the field. It is the best-known **[double move](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move)**,
  a route that shows one break and runs another, and it is aimed at a defender who has been
  breaking on slants all game. Double moves take longer to develop, so they need protection and
  usually a pump fake from the quarterback to sell them; [The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd)
  covers the family.

Two more names are worth having now, though the chapters on concepts develop them. A *drag* or
*shallow cross* runs flat across the field just past the line, under the linebackers
([Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) builds the
[shallow cross](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shallow-cross) concept around it). And a deeper
*crosser* climbs to 12–18 yards on the way across, the route that play-action passes love
([Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)).

## Option routes: the receiver gets a vote

The tree assumes the receiver knows his route before the snap. On an
**[option route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-option-route)** (also called a
**[choice route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-choice-route)**) he doesn't: he picks the
finish after the snap, from what the defense does. The rule is usually something like this:
"Push to six yards. If one man is following you, break away from him, out if he's inside, in if
he's outside. If the defenders are guarding areas, find the hole between them and sit down, facing
the quarterback."

```{python}
#| label: fig-option-route
#| fig-cap: "One option route, two defenses. The slot receiver (Y) pushes to about 6 yards, then decides. Left, man coverage: the nickel defender (\\$) lines up on Y's inside shoulder to take away the middle, so Y breaks out, away from him (the dotted line is the in-cut he would run if the defender were outside). Right, zone: the defenders drop to areas and watch the quarterback, so Y settles in the hole between the hook defender (M) and the curl-flat defender (\\$) and turns to face the quarterback."
def option_play(man):
    off = [p for p in offense("gun_2x2") if p.key in ("C", "RG", "RT", "QB", "Y", "Z")]
    off = [p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=16.0) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
    dfn = [Player("NB", "NB", "def", 1.6 if man else 3.8, 7.6 if man else 11.2, label="$"),
           Player("MIKE", "MIKE", "def", 4.5, 1.5, label="M"),
           Player("RCB", "CB", "def", 7.0, 16.5, label="CB")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    if man:
        p.route("Y", r.path((5.5, 0.0), (6.0, 5.0)))
        p.path("NB", [(5.6, 9.6), (5.9, 12.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.2, delay=0.1)
        p.path("RCB", [(16.0, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)      # carries Z deep
        p.route("Z", r.go(18))
    else:
        p.route("Y", r.path((6.0, 0.0), (5.6, -0.3)))
        p.drop("NB", (6.8, 14.2))
        p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 3.0))
        p.drop("RCB", (15.0, 15.5))
        p.route("Z", r.go(18))
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
for ax, man, ttl in ((axes[0], True, "Against man: break away from him"),
                     (axes[1], False, "Against zone: sit in the hole")):
    p = option_play(man)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-3, 21), window=(-7, 15.5), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    y0 = p.players["Y"]
    if man:
        dotted(fld, p, [(4.8, y0.w), (6.2, y0.w - 4.6)], color=style.MUTED)
        tag(fld, p, "$ sits inside:\nY breaks out", (11.0, 5.0), fs=6.4)
    else:
        tag(fld, p, "Y sits in the hole\nbetween M and $", (11.2, 6.0), fs=6.4)
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Why give the receiver a choice? Because the right route depends on the coverage, and the coverage
isn't settled until after the snap. Against [man coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage),
the defender's position tells you which way he is protecting. A defender standing on the receiver's
inside shoulder is taking away the middle, so the open break is outside, and vice versa. That
position is the defender's [leverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside),
and an option route is built to break away from it: the receiver has what
[Spread Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd) called a
[two-way go](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-way-go), and he uses it. Against
[zone coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-coverage), the defenders are watching the
quarterback rather than the receiver, and nobody follows him, so running away from someone is
pointless. What works is to stop in the space between two of them. One route call, one receiver,
and he is right against both.

The cost is that two people must make the same decision in a split second. If the receiver sees
man and breaks out while the quarterback sees zone and throws to the spot where he should have sat
down, the ball goes to nobody, or to a defender. Option routes therefore go to the receivers a
quarterback trusts most, and teams that rely on them practise them endlessly. The Patriots of the
Tom Brady era were famous for building their passing game around option routes for slot receivers
such as Wes Welker and Julian Edelman.[^patriots] The same idea appears in
[What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), where the tight end's
route on Stick settles against zone and breaks away against man. More broadly, many routes carry
smaller conversion rules ("against a two-deep shell, bend the seam into the middle"), which
[Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) collects as
[route conversions](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-route-conversion).

## The drop: the quarterback's feet are a clock

Now the "when." A quarterback doesn't just walk back and look around. His feet follow a
prescribed pattern called a **[drop](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-drop-3-5-7-step)**, counted
in steps, and each drop is paired with a depth of route.

From [under center](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-under-center), where he takes the snap with
his hands under the center and starts about a yard and a half behind the line, the classic menu is:

- **Three-step drop**: about 5 yards deep, finished a little under a second after the snap. It goes
  with the quick routes that break at 5–6 yards: hitches, slants, quick outs. The ball should leave
  as his third step lands, more or less as the receiver breaks.
- **Five-step drop**: about 7 yards deep, finished in roughly a second and a half. It goes with the
  intermediate routes at 10–14 yards: outs, curls, digs. The quarterback usually adds a short step
  forward at the end of the drop, a *hitch step* (not to be confused with the hitch route), to
  gather himself, and throws.
- **Seven-step drop**: about 9 yards deep, finished in about two seconds. It goes with the deep
  routes at 15–20 yards and beyond: comebacks, posts, corners, deep digs. It is the slowest drop and
  the one that most needs the line to hold, which is a big reason it is rarer now than in the 1970s
  and 80s.

From the [shotgun](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shotgun), the quarterback starts about five
yards deep, so he needs fewer steps to reach the same depths. The pairs become **one, three and
five steps**: a one-step drop (often just a catch, a step and a throw) for the quick game, three
steps for intermediate routes and five for deep ones. The pairing of depth and time stays the same.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drop-timing
#| fig-cap: "Drops and routes are built as pairs. Left: roughly where the quarterback's last step lands for each drop, measured from the line of scrimmage. Shotgun drops are two steps shorter for the same depth because he starts five yards back. Right: the textbook timing of each pair, in seconds after the snap: the quarterback's drop (blue), the receiver's run to his break (green, diamond = the break), and the moment the ball should leave (brown ball). The black tick on each row is the real median time to throw for passes of that depth, 2023-2025, which runs later than the textbook because many throws are not first-read, on-time throws (the chart on progressions shows why). Textbook depths and times are typical values; they vary by team and quarterback."
_tt = reads[(reads.season >= 2023) & reads.air_yards.notna()].dropna(subset=["time_to_throw"])
TTT_MED = {"quick": _tt.loc[_tt.air_yards.between(0, 9), "time_to_throw"].median(),
           "mid": _tt.loc[_tt.air_yards.between(10, 14), "time_to_throw"].median(),
           "deep": _tt.loc[_tt.air_yards >= 15, "time_to_throw"].median()}

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, width_ratios=[1.0, 2.6], wspace=0.08)
axd, axt = fig.add_subplot(gs[0]), fig.add_subplot(gs[1])

# --- left: drop depths
axd.axhline(0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=1.4, alpha=0.75)
axd.text(1.0, 0.35, "line of scrimmage", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2)
DEPTHS = {0: [("start", 1.5), ("3-step", 5.0), ("5-step", 7.0), ("7-step", 9.0)],
          2: [("start", 5.0), ("1-step", 6.0), ("3-step", 7.5), ("5-step", 9.0)]}
for x, lst in DEPTHS.items():
    axd.plot([x, x], [-lst[0][1], -lst[-1][1]], color=style.BASELINE, lw=3, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=1)
    for name, d in lst:
        start = name == "start"
        axd.scatter([x], [-d], s=55 if start else 34, color=style.OFFENSE if start else style.SURFACE,
                    edgecolor=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
        axd.text(x + 0.22, -d, name if not start else "QB starts", fontsize=6.6, va="center", ha="left",
                 color=style.INK if not start else style.INK_2)
axd.set_xticks([0, 2], ["Under\ncenter", "Shotgun"], fontsize=7.2)
axd.set_yticks([0, -3, -6, -9], ["LOS", "3 yd", "6 yd", "9 yd"], fontsize=7)
axd.set_xlim(-0.5, 3.6)
axd.set_ylim(-10.2, 1.4)
axd.grid(False)
axd.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
axd.tick_params(axis="x", length=0)
axd.set_title("Where the drop ends", fontsize=8.6)

# --- right: timing
ROWS = [  # key, label, drop end, set/hitch end, throw, break time, route text
    ("quick", "Quick: 3-step\n(gun: 1-step)", 0.85, 1.0, 1.0, 1.05, "routes at 5-6 yd: hitch, slant, quick out"),
    ("mid", "Intermediate: 5-step\n(gun: 3-step)", 1.45, 1.85, 1.85, 1.95, "routes at 10-14 yd: out, curl, dig"),
    ("deep", "Deep: 7-step\n(gun: 5-step)", 1.95, 2.45, 2.45, 2.6, "routes at 15-20 yd: comeback, post, corner"),
]
for i, (key, lab, drop, hitch, throw, brk, txt) in enumerate(ROWS):
    y = -i * 1.25
    axt.barh(y + 0.2, drop, height=0.26, color=style.OFFENSE, alpha=0.9)
    axt.barh(y + 0.2, hitch - drop, left=drop, height=0.26, color=style.OFFENSE_TINT, edgecolor=style.OFFENSE, lw=0.6)
    axt.barh(y - 0.17, brk, height=0.2, color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.75)
    axt.scatter([brk], [y - 0.17], marker="D", s=30, color=style.THIRD, edgecolor="white", zorder=4)
    axt.scatter([throw], [y + 0.2], marker="o", s=60, color=style.BALL, edgecolor="white", zorder=5)
    axt.plot([TTT_MED[key]] * 2, [y - 0.38, y + 0.42], color=style.INK, lw=1.6, zorder=6)
    axt.text(0.03, y - 0.48, txt, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, va="center")
axt.set_yticks([-i * 1.25 for i in range(3)], [r[1] for r in ROWS], fontsize=7.2)
axt.set_xlim(0, 3.4)
axt.set_ylim(-3.15, 0.65)
axt.set_xlabel("Seconds after the snap", fontsize=7.5)
axt.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
axt.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
axt.yaxis.tick_right()
axt.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
axt.spines["right"].set_visible(True)
axt.set_title("When the ball should come out", fontsize=8.6)
h = [Patch(color=style.OFFENSE, label="QB drop"), Patch(fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT, ec=style.OFFENSE, label="hitch / set"),
     Patch(color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.75, label="receiver to break"),
     Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=style.BALL, label="ball out"),
     Line2D([], [], color=style.INK, lw=1.6, label="real median, 2023-25")]
fig.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.02), ncol=5, fontsize=6.8, frameon=False,
           handlelength=1.4, columnspacing=1.0)
plt.show()
```

Why are drops and routes paired this way? Because both are clocks, and the offense wants them to
ring together. A receiver running at full speed covers 5 yards in about a second and 12 yards in
about two (he starts from a standstill and has to fight a defender on the way). A quarterback
backing up covers 5 yards of drop in about a second and 7 to 9 yards in one and a half to two
seconds. If the two are matched, the quarterback's back foot hits the ground at the moment the
receiver is making his cut, and the ball can leave without a pause. If they are mismatched, one of
them waits. A quarterback who takes a seven-step drop to throw a hitch hands the cornerback two free
seconds to close; a quarterback who takes a three-step drop to throw a post has to stand and hold
the ball while the rush arrives.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Drops turn a judgment ("is he open yet?") into a rhythm ("throw on the fifth step"). A quarterback
who waits to *see* a receiver open is late, because a receiver who looks open has usually been open
for half a second already, and the ball needs another second to get there. A quarterback whose feet
tell him when the receiver will be at his spot can throw before the defender has reacted to the
break. The cost is that a rhythm can be disrupted: a pass rusher in his face, a receiver knocked off
his path at the line, or a defender sitting on the spot breaks the timing, and the quarterback then
has to improvise.
:::

Three complications are worth knowing. **The shotgun changed the picture.** In 2025 about
`{python} f"{GUN_DB_25:.0%}"` of NFL dropbacks started from the shotgun or the pistol.[^gun] A shotgun quarterback sees the
defense better at the snap and reaches his throwing depth sooner, which suits the quick passing game
that dominates the modern NFL. **Play-action changes the footwork.** On a play-action pass the
quarterback fakes a handoff first, often turning his back to the defense, so the "drop" is a fake
plus a setup, and the routes are timed to that longer clock
([Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)). **Not every throw comes
off a drop.** Quarterbacks also roll out, throw on the move, and escape a collapsing
[pocket](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pocket), the protected area the line forms around them;
the routes then follow the scramble rules covered in [Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd).

### Timing routes: throw it before he breaks

Put the pieces together and you get a **[timing route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-timing-route)**:
a route the quarterback throws to a spot at a set moment, as his drop ends and often before the
receiver has made his break. This is the play from the opening paragraph.

```{python}
#| label: fig-timing-route
#| fig-cap: "A timing route: the 12-yard out from a five-step drop under center, against an off cornerback playing a deep third. The ball leaves the quarterback's hand as his back foot settles, a beat before Z has broken toward the sideline, and is thrown to a spot, not to the man. The cornerback can only drive on the ball once Z breaks, so he arrives a step after it. Panels are seconds after the snap (simulated play; Z and the cornerback are ringed)."
def timing_out():
    off = [p for p in offense("singleback") if p.key not in ("H",)]
    dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off)
    keep = {"SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE", "MIKE", "WILL", "FS", "SS", "RCB", "LCB"}
    dfn = [p for p in dfn if p.key in keep]
    mv = {"RCB": (7.5, 15.5), "SS": (6.5, 8.0), "FS": (13.0, 0.0)}
    dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1], label="CB" if p.key == "RCB" else None) if p.key in mv
           else p.moved(label="CB") if p.key == "LCB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.block("Y", pts=[(-0.4, 0.3)])
    p.block("RB", pts=[(1.5, 2.2)])
    p.dropback(5.5)                                    # five steps from under center
    p.path("QB", [(0.8, 0.0)], speed=2.0)              # the hitch step: set and throw
    p.route("Z", r.path((13.5, 0.0), (13.5, 9.5)), speed=6.8)
    p.route("X", r.go(20))
    p.path("RCB", [(15.0, 16.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.0)           # bail to the deep third
    p.path("RCB", [(12.8, 22.6)], absolute=True, speed=6.5, delay=0.75)  # drive once Z breaks
    p.drop("SS", (9.0, 11.0))                          # curl-flat defender gets depth
    p.drop("FS", (16.0, 1.0))
    p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 2.0))
    p.highlight("Z", "RCB")
    p.pass_to("Z", t=1.75)
    return p


tp = timing_out()
TIMES = [0.9, 1.75, 2.2, 3.05]
if PDF:
    with ball_speed(22):
        strip(tp, TIMES,
              ["+0.9 s: Z still looks like a go route", "+1.75 s: back foot down, ball out",
               "+2.2 s: Z breaks, the corner drives", "+3.05 s: catch; the corner is a step late"],
              lateral=(-3, 26.6), window=(-9.5, 18.5), rings=("Z", "RCB"), ncols=2, rulers=False, width_in=5.6)
        plt.show()
else:
    with ball_speed(22):
        show_animation(tp, times=TIMES)
```

Follow the cornerback. At 0.9 seconds he is backpedalling, watching Z run straight at him: as far as
he can tell, this could still be a go route, and if he stops he gets beaten deep. At 1.75 seconds the
quarterback's back foot lands at the end of his five-step drop and he throws, at a spot near the
sideline, 13 or so yards downfield. Z still hasn't cut. Only when Z breaks, at about 2.2 seconds,
can the cornerback stop and drive toward the sideline, and by then the ball is already well on its
way. The receiver catches it about a second later with the cornerback a step behind.

The throw is to a *spot*, not to a man, and it leaves before the receiver gets there. That is what
makes it hard to defend and also what makes it hard to execute: it needs the receiver to be at the
spot on time, at the right depth, every time. A receiver who is jammed at the line and arrives late,
or who rounds his cut and arrives a yard short, turns a completion into an incompletion or, if the
cornerback guessed right, into an interception returned the other way. Coaches use related
words for throws like this: a [rhythm throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rhythm-throw) comes out
on the last step of the drop, with no hitch ([The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd)), and an
[anticipation throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-anticipation-throw) is any throw released
before the receiver is open ([Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd)).

### The clock in real games

The black ticks on the timing chart are a reality check. In 2023–2025 the median throw to a
receiver 10–14 yards downfield left the quarterback's hand about
`{python} f"{TTT_MED['mid']:.1f}"` seconds after the snap, and the median deep throw (15 yards or
more) about `{python} f"{TTT_MED['deep']:.1f}"`. That is later than the textbook, for good reasons.
The medians include every throw: the ones made on time, but also throws to a second or third option
after the first was covered, throws after a scramble, and throws to a back released late. Short
throws are slowest of all relative to their textbook time, because "short" includes
[checkdowns](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown), the short throws to a safe receiver a
quarterback makes after everything else was covered. The textbook clock describes the *plan*; the
data describe the plan plus everything that happened when the plan didn't work. The section on
progressions below measures that difference directly.

### A short history: Walsh and the three-step game

The modern emphasis on timing owes a lot to Bill Walsh. In 1970, Walsh was an assistant on Paul
Brown's Cincinnati Bengals staff, and his starting quarterback, Virgil Carter, was mobile and
accurate but did not have a strong arm. Rather than ask Carter to throw deep, Walsh built a passing
game around short, quick, precisely timed throws, many of them off three-step drops, spread across
the whole width of the field, so that a pass could do the work of a running play. Carter led the NFL
in completion percentage in 1971.[^walsh] Walsh took the approach, much refined, to San Francisco as
head coach in 1979 and won three Super Bowls with it. The family of offenses descended from his work
became known as the **[West Coast offense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-west-coast-offense)**,
the subject of [Offensive Systems and Play-Calling Languages](04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd)
and of the case study [Case Study: Bill Walsh's 49ers and the West Coast Offense](../12-case-studies/12-01-walsh-49ers-west-coast.qmd).
The underlying idea is the one in this section: if the quarterback's feet and the receiver's route
run on the same clock, the ball can leave before the defense has time to react.

## Reads: what the quarterback is looking at

The routes put receivers in places and the drop sets the moment. The quarterback still has to choose.
He makes that choice with a [read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-read-post-snap), a decision made
after the snap by watching something specific, in the form "if this, then that." Pass plays use two
kinds of read, and nearly every play mixes them.

- **A progression read** asks *which receiver is open*, looking at receivers one at a time, in order.
- **A defender read** asks *what is this defender doing*, watching one defender and throwing to the
  receiver he can't cover.

### Progressions

A **[progression](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-progression)** is the order in which the
quarterback looks at his receivers. The play call gives him a first read, usually the route the play
was designed around; if that receiver is covered, he moves his eyes to the second, then the third,
and finally to the checkdown, the short, safe throw to a back or tight end that keeps the play from
losing yards. Coaches often tie each read to the footwork: the first read is thrown on the last step
of the drop, the second on the hitch step, the third after a second hitch, so the progression runs
on the same clock as the drop.

```{python}
#| label: fig-progressions
#| fig-cap: "Two ways to order the quarterback's looks. The numbers are the progression: the order in which he checks receivers. Left, a half-field read: the play is a two-man combination on the right (a corner route over a hitch, both reading the same cornerback) with the back as the outlet; the routes on the left (faded) are only there to occupy defenders, so he can throw from a short drop. Right, a full-field read: he starts deep on the left and works across the field to the checkdown, which needs a deeper drop and more time from the line."
def prog_play(full):
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    off = [p.moved(w=-16.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-8.5) if p.key == "H" else
           p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=16.0) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
    p = Play(off, [], los=35, to_go=None)
    if full:
        p.dropback(4.0)
        p.route("X", r.post(12))
        p.route("H", r.dig(12, 12))
        p.route("Y", r.curl(12))
        p.route("Z", r.comeback(15))
        p.route("RB", r.path((2.0, 5.5), (6.0, 6.5)), side=+1)
        order = [("1", (23.5, -11.0)), ("2", (13.8, 2.0)), ("3", (8.4, 5.4)), ("4", (10.4, 20.2)),
                 ("5", (3.0, 6.0))]
    else:
        p.dropback(2.5)
        p.route("Y", r.corner(10))
        p.route("Z", r.hitch(5))
        p.route("RB", r.path((3.0, 4.0), (6.0, 8.5)), side=+1)
        p.route("X", r.slant(2, 7))
        p.route("H", r.stick(6))
        order = [("1", (22.6, 19.6)), ("2", (6.6, 17.6)), ("3", (3.0, 4.6))]
    return p, order


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.75))
for ax, full, ttl in ((axes[0], False, "Half-field: one side, 1-2-3"), (axes[1], True, "Full-field: left to right, 1-5")):
    p, order = prog_play(full)
    fld = p.draw(ax=ax, lateral=(-21.5, 21.5), window=(-8, 26), title=False)
    no_numbers(ax)
    if not full:   # fade the routes that are not part of the read
        for ln in ax.lines:
            xs = ln.get_xdata()
            if len(xs) and np.mean(xs) < FIELD_W - p.ball_y - 3.5:   # plot-x left of the ball = offense's left
                ln.set_alpha(0.25)
        for pa in ax.patches:
            if isinstance(pa, FancyArrowPatch):
                x_end = pa._posA_posB[1][0] if pa._posA_posB else 0
                if x_end < FIELD_W - p.ball_y - 3.5:
                    pa.set_alpha(0.25)
    for n, at in order:
        x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(*at))
        ax.text(float(x), float(y), n, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5, fontweight="bold", color="white",
                zorder=13, bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.18", fc=style.THIRD, ec="white", lw=0.8))
    ax.set_title(ttl, loc="left", fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```

Progressions come in two sizes.

- **Half-field reads.** The quarterback reads only one side of the field, usually a combination of
  two or three routes built to work together on that side. The other side's routes exist to keep
  defenders busy, or as an emergency answer if the defense blitzes. Half-field reads are fast and
  simple: the quarterback can decide before the snap which side gives the best matchup and then look
  only there. Most of the quick passing game works this way.
- **Full-field reads.** The quarterback starts on one side, often with a deep route, and works across
  the whole field to the checkdown on the other. A full-field progression gives him more options and
  more chances to find the one mistake the defense made, but it needs a deeper drop and more time,
  and moving his eyes and feet across the field takes time the rush may not allow. Full-field reads
  are a mark of experienced quarterbacks and good offensive lines.

The trade between the two is speed versus flexibility. A half-field read gets the ball out quickly,
and a full-field read can beat more coverages. A play-caller picks between them partly on the
situation and partly on the quarterback: a rookie gets more half-field reads; a veteran with a good
line gets the whole field.

#### What the data says about progressions

Since 2022, the charting company FTN has recorded, for every NFL pass, which read in the progression
the ball went to. The nflverse project republishes that charting, so we can see how often
quarterbacks really get past their first look.

```{python}
#| label: fig-reads
#| fig-cap: "Where the ball actually goes in a progression: FTN's charting of 2022-2025 regular-season pass attempts (sacks excluded) by the read the quarterback threw to. Bar length is the share of attempts; the labels give EPA per attempt and the median time from snap to throw. More than half of all throws go to the first read, and they are both the quickest and the most valuable. Every later look costs time and value; checkdowns are completed most often but are worth about nothing. Designed throws (mostly screens) and scramble-drill throws sit outside the progression. Read codes are interpreted as described in the text."
READ_NAMES = {"1": "First read", "2": "A later read", "CHK": "Checkdown", "DES": "Designed throw (screens)",
              "SD": "Scramble drill", "0": "No read (mostly throwaways)"}
rd = (reads[reads.read_thrown.isin(READ_NAMES)]
      .groupby("read_thrown").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"), ttt=("time_to_throw", "median"),
                                  comp=("complete_pass", "mean")))
rd["share"] = rd.n / rd.n.sum()
rd = rd.loc[["1", "2", "CHK", "DES", "SD", "0"]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
ys = np.arange(len(rd))[::-1]
cols = [style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[0], style.MUTED, style.MUTED, style.MUTED]
ax.barh(ys, rd.share, color=cols, height=0.62)
for y, (k, row) in zip(ys, rd.iterrows()):
    ax.text(row.share + 0.008, y, f"{row.share:.0%}   EPA {row.epa:+.2f}   median {row.ttt:.1f} s   "
            f"completed {row.comp:.0%}", va="center", fontsize=6.9, color=style.INK)
ax.set_yticks(ys, [READ_NAMES[k] for k in rd.index], fontsize=7.4)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlim(0, 1.0)
ax.set_xticks([0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6])
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel("Share of pass attempts", fontsize=7.4)
ax.set_title("The progression in the data: early reads are quicker and worth more", fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

The progression shows up clearly. More than half of all throws go to the first read, they come out
fastest, and they are worth the most: the first read is the receiver the play was built to get open,
thrown on time. Each later look costs about half a second and a good chunk of the value, and the
checkdown, while completed most often, is worth roughly nothing on average. (The other categories,
designed throws such as screens and throws made in a scramble, sit outside the progression
altogether.) That is the case for timing in one chart: the offense is at its best when the plan works
the first time.[^ftn]

### Defender reads and the conflict defender

The other kind of read watches one defender instead of a sequence of receivers. The idea is to find
a **[conflict defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-conflict-defender)**, a defender who is
responsible for two things at once, and put two receivers in his area. Whatever he does, he is wrong
about one of them, so the quarterback watches only him and throws to the receiver he leaves. You met
this idea in [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), where the
quarterback on Stick reads the slot defender. The run game uses the same trick on a defender who is
responsible for both a run gap and a pass zone, which is how
[RPOs](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rpo) work ([Run-Pass Options](04-06-rpos.qmd)).

Defender reads are fast, because the quarterback looks at one man, not five, and they don't depend on
the receivers beating anyone. They depend on geometry: a defender can only be in one place. The
offense creates the conflict in one of two directions, up and down or side to side.

## The vertical stretch: high and low

A **[high-low read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-high-low-read)** (also called a
**[vertical stretch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-vertical-stretch)**) puts two receivers in one
defender's area at two depths, one above him and one below. The animation below shows the most common
version, a curl over a flat route, against the defender who guards both in a
[Cover 3](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-3) zone, the
[curl-flat defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat-defender). (Cover 3 has three deep
defenders, each guarding a third of the field's width, and four underneath; you'll meet it properly in
[Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd). For now all that matters is the
one defender.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-high-low
#| fig-cap: "A high-low read of one defender, both branches (simulated play, Cover 3, the right half of the field). Z runs a curl at about 12 yards (high); Y runs to the flat (low). The ringed nickel defender (\\$) is responsible for both areas, so the quarterback watches only him. Top row: he sinks under the curl, so the ball goes to the flat. Bottom row: he jumps the flat, so the ball goes to the curl, behind him and in front of the deep-third cornerback. Times are seconds after the snap."
def high_low(sink):
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    off = [p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=15.5) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
    dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off)
    mv = {"RCB": (7.5, 16.0), "NB": (4.5, 10.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 2.0), "FS": (13.0, 0.0), "SS": (5.0, -11.0),
          "LCB": (7.5, -16.0), "WILL": (4.5, -4.0)}
    dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1]) if p.key in mv else p for p in dfn if p.key != "DB"]
    dfn = [p.moved(label="CB") if p.pos == "CB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    protect(p)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.path("QB", [(0.5, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.route("Z", r.path((12.5, 0.0), (11.2, -1.3)))                     # curl: high
    p.route("Y", r.path((1.0, 3.0), (2.4, 7.5), (3.2, 12.0)), speed=6.4)  # flat: low
    p.path("NB", [(6.5, 11.5)], absolute=True, speed=3.5)               # first steps: shuffle, read
    if sink:
        p.path("NB", [(10.0, 14.0)], absolute=True, speed=4.5)          # sinks under the curl
        p.pass_to("Y", t=1.3)
    else:
        p.path("NB", [(3.8, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=6.5)           # jumps the flat
        p.pass_to("Z", t=1.7)
    p.path("RCB", [(16.0, 17.0)], absolute=True, speed=5.2)             # deep third
    p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 4.0))
    p.route("X", r.go(18))                                              # the left side: just occupying
    p.route("H", r.seam(16))                                            # defenders on the web animation
    p.drop("LCB", (15.0, -16.0))
    p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -4.0))
    p.drop("SS", (7.0, -12.0))
    p.drop("FS", (17.0, 0.5))
    p.highlight("NB")
    return p


HL_SINK, HL_JUMP = high_low(True), high_low(False)
if PDF:
    with ball_speed(22):
        strip([HL_SINK, HL_JUMP], [0.7, 1.3, 2.35, 0.7, 1.7, 2.7],
              ["+0.7 s: $ reads the QB", "+1.3 s: $ sinks; ball to the flat", "+2.35 s: Y catches it",
               "+0.7 s: the same start", "+1.7 s: $ jumps the flat", "+2.7 s: Z catches the curl"],
              lateral=(-2, 26.6), window=(-9.5, 18.5), rings=("NB",), rulers=False,
              notes={1: [("high", (14.3, 11.6)), ("low", (-3.8, 15.5))],
                     4: [("high", (14.3, 11.6)), ("low", (-3.8, 15.5))]})
        plt.show()
else:
    with ball_speed(22):
        show_videos([HL_SINK, HL_JUMP], ["He sinks: throw the flat", "He jumps the flat: throw the curl"])
```

The ringed nickel defender's job in this zone is to guard the area from the sideline in toward the
hash, from the line of scrimmage out to about 12 yards. That is two receivers' worth of field. If he
gets depth to stand under the curl, the flat route is alone in front of him, and the ball goes there
for a few easy yards with room to run. If he comes forward to cover the flat route, the curl settles
in the hole behind him, in front of the cornerback, who is busy guarding the deep third, and the ball
goes there for 10 or 12. The quarterback doesn't need to know the whole coverage; he needs to watch
one man.

Why does this work? Because zone defenders are taught to stay between the ball and the deepest
threat in their area, and to break on the ball when it's thrown. A curl-flat defender who sinks
under the curl is doing his job; he is just losing the flat. The trade is built in. The defense has
three good answers. It can **change who covers what**: in
[man coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage), each receiver has his own defender, and
there's no one to put in conflict (that is why offenses want to know whether the coverage is man or
zone before they choose a read). It can **pattern-match**: zone defenders who are taught to pick up a
receiver who enters their area and stay with him, so the curl-flat defender takes the flat route and a
linebacker gets under the curl ([Cover 3](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) covers the
match rules). Or it can **bait**: show a soft flat, then drive on it once the ball is in the air,
hoping to catch a quarterback who decided too early.

The high-low idea is everywhere. A corner route over a hitch puts a cornerback who plays the flats in
[Cover 2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-2) in the same bind (that is the concept called
[smash](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-smash)), and three receivers at three depths on one sideline
make it a three-level stretch (the [flood](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flood) concept). Both
are built in full in [Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd).

## The horizontal stretch: inside and outside

A **[horizontal stretch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horizontal-stretch)** does the same thing
side to side: it puts receivers on both sides of an underneath defender at about the same depth, so he
can't stand in front of both.

```{python}
#| label: fig-horizontal-stretch
#| fig-cap: "A horizontal stretch. Five receivers settle at 4-6 yards, spread across the field, against the four underneath zone defenders of a Cover 3 defense (dashed arrows are their drops; the two cornerbacks and the free safety bail into the three deep zones). Every underneath defender has a receiver on each side of him. The quarterback watches the ringed Mike: he can't stand in front of both the back (R) and Y, so whichever way he leans (dotted), the man on the other side is open."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [p.moved(w=-16.0) if p.key == "X" else p.moved(w=-8.5) if p.key == "H" else
       p.moved(w=8.5, label="Y") if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(w=15.5) if p.key == "Z" else p for p in off]
dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off)
mv = {"LCB": (8.0, -16.5), "RCB": (8.0, 16.0), "FS": (13.0, 0.0), "SS": (5.5, -11.0),
      "WILL": (4.5, -4.0), "MIKE": (4.5, 1.5), "NB": (4.5, 10.0)}
dfn = [p.moved(d=mv[p.key][0], w=mv[p.key][1], label="CB" if p.pos == "CB" else None) if p.key in mv else p
       for p in dfn if p.key != "DB"]
hz = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=8)
protect(hz)
hz.dropback(2.5)
hz.route("X", r.hitch(5))
hz.route("H", r.path((5.5, -0.8), (5.5, -0.2)))
hz.route("RB", r.path((3.6, -0.6), (9.4, 0.6)), side=+1)       # back checks, then sits over the ball
hz.route("Y", r.path((5.5, 2.5), (5.5, 3.0)), side=-1)        # Y sits just inside, at the hash
hz.route("Z", r.hitch(5))
for k, to in (("LCB", (14.0, -16.5)), ("RCB", (14.0, 16.0)), ("FS", (15.5, 0.0)),
              ("SS", (6.5, -12.0)), ("WILL", (7.0, -5.0)), ("MIKE", (7.0, 1.6)), ("NB", (6.5, 11.5))):
    hz.drop(k, to)
hz.highlight("MIKE")
fld = hz.draw(lateral=(-21.5, 21.5), window=(-8, 16.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld.ax)
ruler(fld, hz, top=15)
dotted(fld, hz, [(7.0, 1.6), (7.4, 4.6)], color=style.DEFENSE)
dotted(fld, hz, [(7.0, 1.6), (7.4, -1.4)], color=style.DEFENSE)
tag(fld, hz, "M leans to Y:\nthrow to R", (10.6, 6.8), fs=6.6)
tag(fld, hz, "M leans to R:\nthrow to Y", (10.6, -4.0), fs=6.6)
plt.show()
```

The arithmetic is the heart of it. A zone defense has only so many underneath defenders: four in
Cover 3, five in Cover 2, after it has spent players on the pass rush and the deep zones. If the
offense puts five receivers across the field at the same depth against four underneath defenders, at
least one receiver has nobody in front of him, and every defender has a receiver on each side. Each
defender who tries to cover two receivers is a conflict defender. The Mike in the figure stands in his
[hook zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hook-zone), the area just past the line in the middle,
with the back sitting on one side of him and Y sitting on the other. If he leans toward Y, the back is
open; if he stays home, Y is.

Horizontal stretches tend to be short throws, because they work underneath, in front of the deep
defenders. That makes them reliable and quick, the backbone of the quick game's
[spacing](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spacing) and [stick](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stick)
concepts ([The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd)). What they give up is depth: a horizontal stretch
rarely produces a big play by itself, and it needs the receiver to make yards after the catch.
Combine a horizontal stretch with a vertical one and you get a triangle of three receivers around one
defender, the [triangle read](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-triangle-read) of
[Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd).

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Stretches are how an offense beats zone coverage without needing to win a one-on-one race. Against
zone the defenders aren't following anyone; they are guarding areas, and areas have edges. Put two
receivers inside one defender's area, one above him or beside him, and he has to choose. This is
Gillman's old principle of making the defense cover the whole field, applied one defender at a time.
Against man coverage, stretches matter less, because there's no area to overload, and the offense's
answer is different: routes that win one-on-one, double moves, and routes that cross so defenders get
in each other's way (the [man-beaters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-beater) of
[Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)). Which is why the question "man or zone?" sits
behind every read, and why the matrix of which concepts beat which coverages waits until the coverages
are taught, in [What Beats What](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd).
:::

## Measuring a throw: air yards, YAC and aDOT

Once the ball is caught, the yards come from two places: the distance the ball traveled in the air,
and the distance the receiver ran after he caught it. Analytics splits them, and the three numbers it
uses appear in broadcasts, box scores and almost every article about a quarterback.

- **[Air yards](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-air-yards)** measure how far past the line of
  scrimmage the ball traveled in the air, to the spot where it was caught, or where the target was
  when it fell incomplete. Only the distance downfield counts, not the sideways distance. A screen
  caught 3 yards behind the line has −3 air yards.
- **[YAC](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yac)**, **[yards after catch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yards-after-catch)**,
  is what the receiver adds from the catch to the end of the play.
- **[aDOT](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-adot)**, **[average depth of target](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-average-depth-of-target)**,
  is the average air yards per pass, for a quarterback (per throw) or a receiver (per target),
  completed or not. It describes *where* a quarterback throws or a receiver is used, not how well.
